newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Dubai company will meet protesters to Safrica deal.
newsitem.headline: Dubai company will meet protesters to Safrica deal.

text.p: A Dubai-based multinational company trying to win commercial control over nature reserves in South Africa has agreed to talk over its deal with protesting environmentalists, authorities announced on Friday.

The Dolphin Group, a major tourism and leisure operator in Africa through its Block Hotels and United Touring Company (UTC), will meet a team of environmental experts in London next week, South African officials said in a statement.

Environmentalists have poured scorn on the deal, signed between Dolphin and the state-owned Mpumalanga Parks Board last November. The deal could be derailed by land claims by blacks who say that they were deprived of territory under apartheid.

The Dolphin Group's Kenyan-born chief executive, Ketan Somaia, publicly reacted to the row on February 19, saying the company's motives were pure and adding: "It is unfortunate that there has been ill-informed comment."
The reserves in question lie in the eastern province of Mpumalanga, home also to South Africa's vast Kruger National Park. Dolphin plans to inject 400 million rand ($84 million) into the project.

Criticism centres on the secrecy which allowed the deal to be signed without prior public debate, a clause apparently allowing profits to be accrued abroad and charges that the parks board had sacrificed too much control to Dolphin.

On Friday, Mpumalanga's Environmental Affairs and Tourism Minister David Mkhwanazi said he would lead a six-member review team including senior environmentalists to London next week, where Somaia was expected to meet them on Wednesday.
"The aim of the negotiations is to discuss with the Dolphin Group a number of issues which have been raised by environmental and commercial lobbies as well as by affected communities.
"We wish to bring development to Mpumalanga. At the same time we need to be mandated by those people whose lives we are affecting," Mkhwanazi said.

Under the deal, Dolphin takes commercial rights to five tourism areas -- including the dramatic red sandstone canyon at Blyde River -- in return for bankrolling the parks board's accumulated deficit for 50 years.
There is also an agreement that blacks living on the borders of the reserves will be given a 20 percent share of development companies to be set up in the target areas.
But these communities could still scupper the project with Dolphin if their land claims, pending against two reserves, succeed. No date has yet been set for the claims to be settled.
